extracted.intended_audience: navigators, ship officers, and mariners intending to find longitude at sea using pendulum watches
extracted.subtask_description: Practical instructions for using pendulum (marine) watches to determine time and thereby compute longitude at sea, including watch care, adjustment to mean time, observation methods (sun/star), and procedures for estimating/compensating watch error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carry at least two watches
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who intend to make use of pendulum watches at sea, must have two of them at least.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have at least two watches so that if one fails by accident, neglect, or long use there remains another for use. (Original: 'they must have two of them at least, that, if one of them should by accident or neglect, or long use, happen to fail, there may still remain one for use.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Know watch mechanism and operation
rubrics_metrics.description: Procure good information of the nature of the inward parts of the watches, the manner of winding them, and how to set the indexes or hands having the hours, minutes, seconds, &c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Users should understand watch construction and operation (winding, setting hands) to reduce misuse and be able to adjust or restart them correctly on board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mount watches in a protected, dry location aboard
rubrics_metrics.description: The watches on ship-board are to be hung in a close place, where they may be most free from moisture or dust, and out of danger of being disordered by knocking or touching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep pendulum watches in a sheltered, dry location and avoid places where they can be jarred, struck, or exposed to dust and moisture which will alter their rate or stop them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust watches to keep mean (equal) time before boarding
rubrics_metrics.description: Before the watches be brought on ship-board, they should be adjusted to keep mean time, the use of them being then most easy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If time or convenience prevents full adjustment, watches may still be used provided you know how much they gain or lose in 24 hours (daily rate). Adjustment ashore to mean time is preferable to reduce at-sea corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulate to mean time using equation of time and meridian observations
rubrics_metrics.description: To adjust or regulate the watches to keep equal or mean time: take notice of the equation of time and set watches accordingly; observe the sun on the meridian using a simple meridian line and plummets to check and compute daily difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a table of the equation of time for the year to convert apparent solar time to mean time when setting the watch. Procedure given: set watch by sun minus the equation for that day (example: 12 March equation 8m 3s, so set to 11h 51m 57s), then after several days observe again, add that day's equation to the watch reading, compare to true noon, divide any difference by number of days between observations to obtain daily error (gain/loss per 24h). To improve adjustment, change the small weight on the pendulum: moving the weight down makes the watch slower, up makes it faster. (Note in original: a general table of the equation of time was inserted but was erroneous and omitted here; each year requires its own table.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure daily rate while at anchor using morning/evening or equal-altitude observations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a vessel rides at anchor (harder under sail), observe the sun when half above the horizon in morning and evening (or two equal altitudes) to estimate the daily difference of the watch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: note watch reading when sun is half above horizon in morning; note again at evening when sun half below horizon; compute elapsed watch time between observations, take half and add to morning observation to get watch time of local noon, then add equation of that day to compare to true noon. Repeat after days and divide difference by days to get daily rate. Alternatively use two equal altitudes instead of rising/setting. Refraction errors are small and may be neglected for these methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use watches to find longitude by comparing local apparent time with watch time
rubrics_metrics.description: To find at sea the longitude of the place where you are: before sailing set watches to the (mean) time of the place of departure; at sea observe local time by sun or stars and compare with watch (adjusted for daily rate and equation) to compute longitude difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: set watches ashore to local (departure) time allowing for equation; at sea, observe local time precisely by sun or stars and note watch time (adjusted by known daily error and equation of present day). Difference in hours × 15 degrees = longitude difference (1 hour = 15°; 1 minute = 15' of arc or 1/4°). If local observed time is greater than watch time you are east of departure meridian; if less you are west.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find accurate local time at sea by appropriate observations (avoid unreliable methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: To find the time of the day at sea precisely, do not rely solely on sun's greatest altitude (noon), sea-compasses, or ordinary sun-dials; prefer observing sun's altitude in east/west or using other methods given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sun's altitude near meridian changes slowly so is not precise for minutes/seconds; astronomical rings and common sun-dials are insufficient. Better to observe the sun's altitude when in the east or west (where altitude changes rapidly) and compute hour from pole height and sun declination, or use the rising/setting or equal-altitude methods described. These give the necessary precision because 1 minute error corresponds to 1/4° of longitude (~15 miles at equator).

rubrics_metrics.name: Find longitude via rising/setting observations and watches (simple method needing no instruments)
rubrics_metrics.description: A method that requires only observing the sun's rising and setting (when half above horizon) and using the watches to derive local noon and thus longitude; does not require knowledge of pole height, declination, or astronomical instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: mark watch times at rising and setting (half above/below horizon), compute elapsed time between observations and take half to get time of local noon by watch, add equation of day. If sum equals 12h you are under same meridian as watch origin; if greater or less, convert the difference to degrees (×15° per hour). This method avoids significant refraction error because morning/evening refractions are nearly equal at sea. Variants: observe setting then next morning rising; observe two equal altitudes before/after noon; when sailing north/south observe when sun due east/west.

rubrics_metrics.name: When multiple watches diverge, prefer the fastest and understand causes
rubrics_metrics.description: If watches that have gone exactly for a while should afterwards differ from one another, it will be best to reckon by that which goes fastest, unless there is an apparent cause why it goes too fast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: pendulum suspending wire may stretch (making watches slow) but cannot shorten; the little pendulum weight may slip downwards (making watch faster) but cannot slip upwards. Thus a faster watch is more likely to reflect true time when divergence occurs. Inspect for apparent mechanical causes before deciding.
